e3.reason: The statement is conditional ('when a collection has been counted correctly') and says what the last word means; it does not require the learner to be able to execute the tagging. Only the test, where the child itself counts 7 blocks, needs one-to-one tagging. Would become necessary if 'counted correctly' must be something the learner itself can produce.

e5.reason: The invariance claim is about the number found by counting a collection; counting.objects already presupposes the last-word idea (e9), so the dependence on last-word runs through counting.objects.

e18.reason: Reading a numeral needs the spoken word for each digit, but not the ordered recitation of the list; the words could be learned numeral by numeral. The test also includes 0, whose word is outside counting.sequence.recite (which starts at one).
e18.would_decide: Whether the map wants a separate number-word vocabulary node (including zero) distinct from the ordered list, or evidence that children can read numerals 1-9 without being able to recite 1-9 in order.

e19.reason: Finding which set has 4 can be done by counting, but the sets in the test (3, 4, 5) are small.
e19.other_route: Subitize each small set (about 5 or fewer) and compare its name to the numeral, via subitizing.perceptual, with no counting.

e21.reason: Writing a numeral for a spoken number and reading a numeral are the two directions of one word-symbol association. Production can be learned (by tracing and copying) without ever being tested on recognition, so neither strictly requires the other.

e25.reason: Conceptual subitizing needs some way to get from recognized parts (5 and 2) to the whole 7, but join-and-count-all is only one such means, and the point of the node is to know the whole without counting it.
e25.would_decide: Whether children at this level typically get the whole by a prior join-and-count-all experience, or by recognizing the pattern or counting on; if count-all is the only available means of composing at level 1, the edge is necessary.

e26.reason: Number-composition within 5 is the symbolic, no-arrangement version of what conceptual subitizing does with arrangements. The test uses 5 and 2 giving 7, beyond within-5, and the dependence plausibly runs the other way (seeing 5 as 2 and 3 builds the fact).

e28.reason: The wordless apprehension of an exact small quantity is one way to judge sameness by looking.
e28.other_route: Subitize and name each set (subitizing.perceptual), then compare the two names ('three' and 'three').

e29.reason: The procedure counts each set and compares the counts; it can be run without understanding that spreading or reordering leaves the number unchanged. The invariance explains why spread is irrelevant and protects against the perceptual distractor in the test, but is not a step.

e32.reason: 'Later in the count means more' is grounded here by successor (each word is one more).
e32.other_route: The same rule can be established empirically by matching sets (comparing.count.matching) and noticing that the set with leftovers has the later count.

e35.reason: Attending to one attribute among several is the general case of which length is an instance. A child can separate length from weight through experience with long and short things without a general attribute-naming skill.

e37.reason: Substantively right: the stone versus sponge test requires weight as an attribute separate from size. But 'measurement.weight.attribute' does not appear in index.txt; the node must be created or the edge repointed.

e42.reason: The statement and test supply the sets already built ('put 3 counters on a plate, then add 2 more'); finding the total does not need the learner to build a set of a given size. Needed when addends are given as numbers, as in the story node, where it belongs.

e44.reason: The statement and test have the starting set and the removal supplied; counting what remains does not require counting out a given number. Needed when the amounts are given as numbers, as in the take-from story node.

e47.reason: This is a justification of why the whole exceeds the part; the target is a level 1 concept and does not require it. Matching is one way of grounding 'has more'.
e47.other_route: Containment reasoning (the whole includes the part and more), or grounding 'more' by counting or perceptual comparison.

e48.reason: The node needs the notion of 'has more', not the perceptual skill, which only works when one set is about twice the other; the test sets (7 and 4) are not.
e48.other_route: Ground 'has more' by matching, counting, or direct containment reasoning instead.

e49.reason: Joining and counting is one way a learner comes to know the whole of two parts; the target is a no-counting fact.
e49.other_route: Learn the pairs by seeing small sets as arrangements of parts (finger, dice or dot patterns; subitizing.conceptual).

e52.reason: Taking away and counting what is left is one way the missing part is found; the node is two facts (whole from parts, part from whole), and each can be reached another way.
e52.other_route: Find the missing part by thinking 'what joins with 2 to make 5' via join-and-count-all (addition.add-to.count-all), or by pattern recognition of parts.

e53.reason: Dealing one at a time is executable without a check on equality; the matching idea justifies why the shares come out equal. Credit in the test is for 4 per bear made by dealing, not for the justification.

e55.reason: Judging two things alike in some respect is the general ability; identity and shape matching are earlier-appearing special cases and do not require a general classification skill.

e58.reason: Rejecting a curved-sided or open lookalike can be done by attending to straight sides and closure, but that is not the only way.
e58.other_route: Holistic visual comparison with many varied labelled examples and non-examples (typical in curricula), without counting or attending to sides.

e62.reason: Comparing two lengths by aligning ends is the one-dimensional case of comparing by superposition, which is what the target does for whole shapes. The overlay judgment (this part sticks out) does not require the separate length-comparison skill.

e63.reason: Shapes.match ignores size and orientation (same shape, any size); the target requires exact sameness of size and every part. The tolerant concept is neither needed for nor the same as the exact one, and a learner can check identical copies without it.

e64.reason: Overlaying needs turning or flipping, but the statement gives overlay only as an example method.
e64.other_route: Check corresponding parts one at a time (count sides, compare side lengths) while the shapes stay in place, via shapes.sides.count and comparing.size.direct.

e65.reason: Joining sticks end to end creates the corners automatically. Knowing how many sides the shape has (e67) suffices to build it; corner knowledge helps check the figure but is not required.

e72.reason: Covering a shape along drawn lines is one of the two ways the statement allows.
e72.other_route: Name the smaller shapes from the drawn line without covering, which needs recognizing them (shapes.recognize).

e73.reason: Naming the triangles from a diagonal cut (right isosceles, turned) needs more than naming typical examples in usual orientation; the naming route runs through shapes.recognize, which itself builds on the names. Note that the test asks for naming and showing, stricter than the statement's 'or'.

e74.reason: Recognizing the pieces is needed for the naming route only.
e74.other_route: Cover the shape with smaller pieces (shapes.compose.fill-outline) and show it, with no naming of the parts.

The test includes 0, whose spoken word and meaning are not in counting.sequence.recite, which starts at one.

The meaning of 'more' (as opposed to bigger or longer) is assumed by every comparison node but has no node.
